calibration.note: A prior calibration used fixed small iteration counts (200-6000) as a proxy for 'effort', reasoning that a quick attempt should fail and a tuned attempt should pass. A real reviewer measured that this proxy was wrong: grading gives match() a genuine wall-clock budget (up to 90s), and even a plain best-fit-decreasing-seeded hill climb with NO annealing sophistication (never accepts a worse move) can run hundreds of thousands of cheap iterations in 30s alone, reaching 1,633,947 cents on the held-out scenario -- comfortably clearing the previous 2,030,000 bar despite being, in the reviewer's words, 'a standard algorithms-course exercise.' Recalibrated using the SAME plain hill-climb algorithm but given the full realistic grading budget (75s of the 90s window): measured directly, it plateaus at 1,618,185 cents (6.4% of total value) and does NOT improve meaningfully with more time (measured at 10s/30s/60s/75s budgets: 1594183/1672061/1611712/1618185 -- flat, confirming this is a genuine local-optimum ceiling for plain hill-climbing, not a slow-converging line that more budget would eventually cross). An adaptive simulated-annealing implementation (cooling rate computed from a live per-customer calibration burst so it decays to near-zero exactly at the deadline, rather than a fixed decay constant tuned for one iteration count) was measured at the same 75s budget and reaches 927,470 cents (3.7%) -- a robust, budget-independent 1.7x gap that held up (1.2x-1.7x) across additional scenarios swept at shorter budgets too. The new pass bar sits between these two, close to the annealing reference, well below the plain-hill-climb ceiling regardless of how much of the time budget that ceiling is given.
